22040872.title: Mathematical performance and long-term memory for numbers
22040872.description: Abstract Despite extensive research on the cognitive basis for mathematical activity, the associations between long-term memory and math skills remain relatively understudied. In our fuzzy-trace theory-driven study, we addressed this issue by investigating the relationships between long-term memory for numbers and prominent math skills, namely approximate number processing, arithmetic fluency, and math reasoning, along with math self-concept. Individuals who performed better in the numerical memory task demonstrated better math reasoning, a higher math self-concept, and were more arithmetically fluent. We did not find an association between memory and approximate number processing. Crucially, our memory task, based on the conjoint recognition model, allowed us to go beyond merely measuring overall performance and, as a result, to test fine-grained memory processes related to two memory traces: verbatim (remembering exact numbers) and gist (remembering a general intuition about a number's magnitude). While both gist and verbatim processes correlated with math reasoning, the associations involving gist-based processes were more prominent, which is consistent with one of the main assumptions of fuzzy-trace theory. This pattern was further supported by the results of the cluster-based analysis. On the other hand, even though math self-concept was positively associated with overall numerical memory performance, it correlated significantly only with verbatim-based process. Overall, our study shows the nuanced role of long-term memory processes in mathematical skills and demonstrates the power of fuzzy-trace theory and multinomial processing tree modeling in the fine-grained investigation of mathematical cognition. Published paper Obidziński, M., Bażela, N., & Hohol, M. (2025). More gist, better math: Fuzzy-trace theory-based investigation of the relationship between long-term memory and mathematical skills. Cognition , 263 , 106212, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2025.106212 Content This project includes materials and data from a study designed to test the relationship between numerical long-term memory and various mathematical skills, including approximate number processing, arithmetic fluency, and math reasoning, along with math self-concept.  This Zenodo record is an archival copy of the research project originally published in the Open Science Framework under DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/ZTKQA. 22048304.title: Understanding agroforestry tree preferences in Kenya using a Discrete Choice Experiment
22048304.description: Land degradation and increasing climate variability pose significant challenges to smallholder agricultural productivity and rural livelihoods in Kenya. Agroforestry is increasingly promoted as a strategy for addressing these challenges, but the effectiveness and sustained adoption of agroforestry interventions depend on how well proposed tree species and management options align with farmers’ ecological, productive, and livelihood priorities. This dataset was collected to examine smallholder farmers’ preferences for agroforestry attributes and to investigate heterogeneity in these preferences among forest-dependent communities in the Mount Kenya forest ecosystem. The dataset contains survey data from 400 households located in communities adjacent to forests in Meru and Laikipia Counties, Kenya. The household survey collected information on demographic and socioeconomic characteristics, agricultural production and landholdings, household food security, forest-resource use, participation in participatory forest management and community forest organizations, tree planting and agroforestry practices, and perceptions of tree and agroforestry attributes. Farmers also evaluated the importance of agroforestry characteristics using five-point Likert scales. A discrete choice experiment was incorporated into the household survey to elicit preferences for alternative agroforestry systems. The experiment included five attributes: inclusion of fruit trees, effects on crop productivity, value of marketable tree products, adaptability of tree species to local ecological conditions, and seedling price. The experimental design comprised 16 choice sets divided into two blocks, with each household completing eight choice tasks. The dataset therefore contains the household-level characteristics, preference measures, experimental responses, and associated variables needed to reproduce analyses of farmers’ stated agroforestry preferences. The data support analysis of preference heterogeneity across households, including comparisons by gender and participation in participatory forest management. In the associated study, mixed logit models show that productivity and adaptability to local ecological conditions are among the most important determinants of agroforestry preferences, while preferences for fruit-tree inclusion vary substantially across respondents and demographic groups. The dataset provides opportunities for further research on agricultural technology choice, agroforestry adoption, restoration preferences, gender differences in land-use decisions, participatory forest management, and the design of context-specific restoration interventions in smallholder farming systems.

22088394.title: Microfinance et entrepreneuriat des jeunes diplômés dans les régions du Sahara marocain : rôle de l'accompagnement numérique dans la création et la pérennisation d'entreprises formelles et durables
22088394.description: Cet article examine l'impact conjoint de la microfinance et de l'accompagnement numérique sur la création d'entreprises formelles et leur pérennité chez les jeunes diplômés des provinces sahariennes marocaines. Ancré dans un paradigme positiviste et une démarche hypothético-déductive, il propose un modèle conceptuel original articulant 7 construits latents, 39 items de mesure et 15 hypothèses causales, organisés en antécédents (microfinancement, accompagnement numérique, compétences entrepreneuriales numériques, orientation entrepreneuriale, capital social numérique), variable médiatrice (création d'entreprise formelle) et variable finale (pérennité). Les données proviennent d'une enquête auprès de 320 jeunes diplômés des régions de Laâyoune-Sakia El Hamra, Dakhla-Oued Ed-Dahab et Guelmim-Oued Noun, traitées sous SPSS v.26 et SmartPLS 4.0 (bootstrapping 5 000 sous-échantillons). Douze des 15 hypothèses sont validées ; trois sont infirmées, dont l'effet direct du microfinancement sur la pérennité, entièrement médiatisé par la création formelle (H9). L'accompagnement numérique modère positivement l'effet du microfinancement (H3) et exerce un effet plus fort sur la pérennité dans les zones enclavées (H15). La qualité du modèle est satisfaisante (R²_CEF = 0,584 ; R²_PDE = 0,497 ; Q² > 0). Des implications théoriques et managériales sont proposées pour les institutions de microfinance, les Centres régionaux d'investissement et les dispositifs publics d'accompagnement dans les provinces du Sud.
keywords: Microfinance, entrepreneuriat des jeunes diplômés, accompagnement numérique, création d'entreprises formelles, pérennité entrepreneuriale.

22097143.title: Housing conditions, residents' attitudes and preferences towards investments in multi-apartment buildings in Poland and Czechia: ENBLOC survey and discrete choice experiment data

22102640.title: Supporting Information and Computational Data for Thermodynamics of Solvent Competition in Mixed Carbonate Lithium-Ion Solvation: A DFT Study of Li⁺(EC)4-n(DMC)n Complexes
22102640.description: This dataset contains the Supporting Information and computational files associated with the study “Thermodynamics of Solvent Competition in Mixed Carbonate Lithium-Ion Solvation: A DFT Study of Li + (EC) 4-n (DMC) n Complexes.” The study examines the stepwise replacement of ethylene carbonate (EC) by dimethyl carbonate (DMC) in salt- and additive-free Li + (EC) 4-n (DMC) n microsolvation complexes (n = 0–4). Geometry optimizations and analytical frequency calculations were performed at the M06-2X/def2-SVP level with SMD solvation, followed by M06-2X/def2-TZVPP/SMD single-point energy and Natural Bond Orbital (NBO) calculations. The calculated stepwise Gibbs free-energy changes are -0.58, +0.39, -2.84, and +0.50 kcal mol -1 for n = 1–4, respectively. The overall minimum occurs at n = 3, where Li + (EC)(DMC) 3 lies 3.03 kcal mol -1 below Li + (EC) 4 under the adopted computational conditions. The dataset also includes a paired comparison of inner-shell Li + (EC) 3 (DMC) and outer-shell Li + (EC) 3 ···DMC, together with six nominally outer-shell Li + (EC) 3 ···(DMC) 2 starting topologies and their unconstrained optimized structures. Five of the six starting topologies underwent inward migration of one DMC molecule during optimization. Only the same-EC-associated topology retained both DMC molecules outside the first coordination shell, and this structure lies 8.53 kcal mol -1 above the lowest-energy optimized structure in that set. Included materials comprise the final Supporting Information, Gaussian input and output files, optimized Cartesian coordinates, thermochemical data, final single-point energies, NBO analyses, thermodynamic and electronic-descriptor tables, and representative counterpoise calculations. The calculated basis-set superposition errors are 0.51 kcal mol -1 for inner-shell Li + (EC) 3 (DMC) and 0.40 kcal mol -1 for outer-shell Li + (EC) 3 ···DMC. The NBO quantities are provided as comparative electronic descriptors and are not additive components of the calculated Gibbs free energies or a formal energy decomposition. The calculations represent equilibrium-state rankings within a static, salt- and additive-free microsolvation model. They do not provide kinetic barriers, exchange pathways, residence times, or quantitative bulk-electrolyte populations. Author: Bruce M. Prince Affiliation: Department of Chemistry, Texas Southern University, Houston, Texas, USA

22124916.title: Age-Related Differences in Generative Styles During Adulthood: Analysis Dataset
22124916.description: This dataset contains the anonymized individual-level data underlying the analyses reported in the associated manuscript examining age-related differences in four generative styles during adulthood. The data were collected between 2021 and 2023 from a sample of Spanish adults aged 35–65 years. The analytical sample comprises 367 participants distributed across three age groups: 35–45 years (n = 139), 46–55 years (n = 144), and 56–65 years (n = 84). 22165854.title: Data and code for "Can Public Procurement Promote Organic Farming? Evidence From a Cross-Country Factorial Survey Experiment"
22165854.description: Data and replication code for a cross-country factorial survey experiment (FSE) on stakeholder preferences for organic public food procurement policy packages. Stakeholders involved in public food procurement and public catering in Czechia, Germany, Hungary, Poland, and the United Kingdom each evaluated eight randomized procurement policy scenarios. Every scenario varied four policy attributes: * minimum organic content requirement: none, 10%, 40% or 70%; * local/regional sourcing criterion: required or not required; * support for organic product use:  none, advisory services, network and value-chain development, or a comprehensive program combining both; * cost management:  market-priced organic costs, or public funding covering the organic surcharge. Respondents rated each scenario on three 0–10 scales: perceived fairness , perceived effectiveness in promoting organic farming, and perceived  political feasibility . The design is a full factorial of 4 × 2 × 4 × 2 = 64 scenarios, divided into eight balanced blocks of eight. Each respondent was randomly assigned to one block and saw its scenarios in randomized order, yielding a panel structure of evaluations nested within respondents. Fieldwork ran from November 2024 to July 2025 on the SurveyEngine platform. The questionnaire was developed in English and translated and adapted by native experts in each country, with several rounds of qualitative pretesting. The analysis sample comprises 1,281 respondents and 10,248 vignette evaluations (Poland: 552, Czechia: 484, United Kingdom: 87, Hungary: 79, Germany: 79). This is a targeted stakeholder sample rather than a population sample, and recruitment strategies differed across countries. Contents:  Survey data as Excel workbooks, one pair per country: a vignette file recording which of the 64 designed scenarios each respondent saw, and a covariate file with consent, screening, socio-demographics, knowledge checks, all 24 scenario ratings and debriefing items. Each workbook carries the SurveyEngine data dictionary as a second sheet, in the language fielded in that country. The English master questionnaire is included as a Word document: welcome and consent screens, screening and stakeholder questions, the explanation of public procurement and organic farming shown to respondents, the attribute and level table used to build the vignettes, an example vignette, the three evaluation criteria, and the socio-demographic, knowledge-check and debriefing blocks. Three R scripts reproduce the published results: the weighted multivariate ordered probit models on the full sample (pooled, country-specific, and the SUR-style Gaussian robustness models), the same suite on the restricted sample of respondents closest to procurement who passed both knowledge checks, and the post-estimation code for the average discrete changes in the paper's main figure. 22187281.description: Derived data, per-track model predictions, and analysis tables supporting the manuscript  Arousal is envelope, valence is structure: a source-separation study of where musical emotion lives  (submitted to PeerJ Computer Science). All 3,232 clips of MERGE Audio Balanced were separated into four stems (vocals, drums, bass, other) with Hybrid Demucs  hdemucs_mmi , then recombined into 16 conditions to ask where in a mixture the arousal and valence signals actually live. Rather than treating audio as one undifferentiated signal, the study measures both  sufficiency  (can a stem alone predict emotion?) and  necessity  (does removing it cost anything?), which dissociate sharply. The sharpest single result comes from the spectral-shuffle null (Control C3), which preserves a recording's energy envelope while destroying all fine spectral structure. On the official split, it reproduces  82% of the mix's arousal R²  (0.374 of 0.455) but only  19% of its valence R²  (0.033 of 0.179); the artist-disjoint split gives 76% and 15%. Arousal rides largely on the energy envelope while valence requires spectral structure — which is why the intuitive percussion-versus-harmony account of the arousal/valence asymmetry does not survive testing. The condition-level numbers behind this are in  table3_artifact_null.csv . Licence Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International (CC BY-NC 4.0). 23054130.title: Replication material for: Intersectional representative bureaucracy in Europe
23054130.description: EU citizens hold equal welfare rights across Member States, but national bureaucracies implement these rights unequally. We ask whether representative bureaucracy can reduce this inequality, while considering its intersectional nature. Theoretically, we distinguish additive intersectional representation, where shared traits accumulate, from categorical intersectional representation, where specific identity configurations matter. We show how to test both quantitatively. A conjoint experiment with 2,402 public employees in four Western European countries examines their responses to hypothetical social welfare applicants, varying by age, gender, French or Bulgarian origin and integration effort – traits that can match bureaucrats' own lived experiences. We find that male, Bulgarian and poorly integrated applicants are less likely to be prioritised overall, and that single-trait matches leave priorisation largely unchanged. However, prioritisation rises from 49 to 56 per cent as applicants share up to five traits with bureaucrats. Male Bulgarian applicants benefit specifically when assessed by male bureaucrats with a migration background. Both intersectionality models therefore yield distinct and valuable insights, rather than one being analytically superior to the other. Differentiated implementation of EU social rights thus also arises within administrations, through individual bureaucrats' discretion. Intersectional representative bureaucracy may help address resulting inequities—but policy implications require more investigation.

Respondents were informed that responses were anonymous and used only for research, and gave explicit consent to the processing of data on political opinions and on opinions concerning gender identity and sexual orientation. 23388913.title: quant_eval Paired degradation statistics
23388913.description: 48 rows by 28 columns. One row per published run per task family: the paired pass-rate difference between the quantized and full-weight runners with a 95% confidence interval, the two-sided exact McNemar test, the complete discordance breakdown, and a semantic-cluster-adjusted delta and interval. Every row is recomputable in full from the per-case results dataset (D1) using the published gate definitions. The pass counts, deltas, and the entire discordance table follow directly from the per-case outcomes; no intermediate artifact is required. The cluster-adjusted columns are published alongside the row-level statistics rather than in place of them. One task family contains semantic duplicates among its fixtures, so row-level intervals and p-values may be optimistic if the duplicates are dependent. Publishing both, side by side, lets a reader see where a row-level result does not survive clustering — a self-audit no competing evaluation currently performs. Headline result: on Mistral-Nemo-Instruct-2407, evaluated against an identical F16 baseline on identical fixtures, the number of task families showing a statistically significant difference is six of eight at Q4_K_M, zero of eight at Q5_K_M, and zero of eight at Q8_0. The behavioral cost of quantization on this model is incurred almost entirely in the single step from Q5_K_M to Q4_K_M, while most of the storage saving is already banked at Q5_K_M. About the corpus: six published runs across four base models, six model-precision pairs, and three quantization schemes. Mistral-Nemo-Instruct-2407 at Q4_K_M, Q5_K_M, and Q8_0 against an identical F16 baseline; Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B-1M, and Qwen2.5-32B at Q4_K_M against their own F16 baselines. All four models are Apache-2.0. Limits: the Qwen scale ladder is confounded — the 7B run used local llama.cpp with a fixed seed, while the 14B-1M and 32B runs used Modal, which records seed status as "unsupported". Scale and substrate are not separated by this corpus. Cross-model comparison of absolute pass rates is confounded by temperature, which follows each publisher's own model card. Within-run pairing is unaffected, which is what the paired test requires. The fuzz family is an adaptive trajectory; its paired test compares complete-case outcomes, not identical post-divergence prompts. Version 1.0.1 (2026-10-15) corrects README.md: the Figure 1 alt text said Q4_K_M shows large negative differences in six families; it now says five, with one significant improvement (json_multistep). No data file or figure changed. Licence: CC BY 4.0. No model weights are redistributed. Part of the quant_eval public corpus.

23687215.title: Welfare expert evaluation of individual broiler welfare indicators and multidimensional welfare situations
23687215.description: Description This dataset contains expert-elicitation data collected to investigate approaches for aggregating animal-based welfare indicators into an overall welfare assessment for broiler chickens. Two complementary elicitation approaches were used: an indicator-based survey and a situation-based survey. The two approaches were completed by different groups of animal-welfare experts. All published respondent identifiers are anonymized. Indicator-based survey Experts evaluated individual welfare indicators and, where applicable, different severity levels. For each indicator or indicator level, experts provided a welfare impairment score on a 0–100 scale, where 0 represented no welfare impairment and 100 maximal welfare impairment. Experts also assessed the relevance of each indicator for overall welfare assessment and their certainty in the assessment, both on 0–100 scales. In total, 11 welfare indicators were evaluated. Responses are provided in broiler_welfare_indicator_evaluation.csv in long format, with one row per respondent × indicator × level. Twenty experts completed this section. A separate section asked experts to select 10 suitable welfare indicators from a broader list of 26 candidate indicators and assign each selected indicator an importance score between 0 and 100. These responses are provided in broiler_welfare_preference_evaluation.csv . Situation-based survey The situation-based survey used paired comparisons of multidimensional welfare situations. Each comparison consisted of Situation A and Situation B, described by values for multiple welfare indicators. The indicators included in this survey were selected based on the indicator-based survey, resulting in a subset of 10 indicators; flock distribution was excluded. The experimental design consisted of 300 comparison tasks organized into 30 groups of 10 tasks. A partial-profile design was used, meaning that only a subset of indicators differed between the two situations within each task, while the remaining indicators could have identical values. For each comparison, respondents indicated which situation represented poorer welfare and rated the perceived magnitude of the welfare difference on a 0–100 scale. Responses are provided in broiler_welfare_situation_evaluation.csv . Each task_id can be linked to broiler_welfare_situation_design.csv , which describes the indicator values presented in Situations A and B. The design file is provided in long format, with one row per task × situation × indicator. Included files broiler_welfare_indicator_evaluation.csv broiler_welfare_preference_evaluation.csv broiler_welfare_situation_evaluation.csv broiler_welfare_situation_design.csv data_dictionary.csv about_situation_indicators_broilers.html methodology.md The dataset is provided in cleaned and standardized formats to support reuse and further research on animal-welfare assessment and aggregation.

23719183.title: Replication Package: Measuring the Inalienability Boundary of Neurorights - A Discrete Choice Experiment with a Protest Option
23719183.description: Replication package for the DCE-Neurorights study, which measures public preferences over neurodata uses and locates the inalienability boundary at which respondents reject any compensation. 23732997.title: Replication materials: capability labels as behavioral interventions in brain-computer interfaces
23732997.description: Replication materials supporting a manuscript examining whether capability judgments produced by neural-decoding systems should be audited for their behavioral consequences, not only their statistical errors. The package contains analysis code and derived data for three empirical studies: (1) a fixed-pipeline decoding analysis computing per-participant capability labels from three public motor-imagery BCI datasets (PhysioNet EEGMMI n=109; Cho2017 n=52; Lee2019/OpenBMI n=54) under two fixed classifiers (CSP+linear SVM; EEGNet v4); (2) a preregistered randomized vignette survey (N=1,077 analyzed) crossing label presence, label level, and presentation wording, with de-identified cleaned responses and primary, extended, and robustness analysis scripts; (3) a semi-structured stakeholder interview study, reported in aggregate in the manuscript supplement (interview data not shared). Raw EEG data are public and must be obtained from their original repositories; the raw survey export and interview materials are not shared under the approved ethics protocol. See README.md and CODEBOOK.md in the archive. Preregistered at osf.io/j2hbm before outcome data collection.

23735537.title: Data and code for "Cognitive Biases in Large Language Models for Disaster Management: A Controlled Vignette Experiment"
23735537.description: LLM responses and analysis code for the study "Cognitive Biases in Large Language Models for Disaster Management: A Controlled Vignette Experiment" (Idan-Chaim Cohen, Noya Littor, Aviad Elyashar, Rami Puzis, Odeya Cohen; International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction, manuscript IJDRR-D-26-02470; preprint: SSRN abstract 7270406). Six vignette experiments adapted from Roberts and Wernstedt (2019) test six cognitive biases (framing effect, omission-commission regret, attribution bias, frequency-format effect, neighbor effect, outcome bias) in eight LLMs from four providers across three hazard scenarios (earthquake, wildfire, chemical spill). The record contains the February-April 2026 responses (100 valid responses per model, vignette and experiment), the September-October 2026 alternative-wording run on four models (raw and cleaned files), the 108 prompts of that run, refusal counts, the derived tables of the revision, and the analysis notebook and scripts. README.md describes every file and column and gives the reproduction steps. Data: CC BY 4.0. Code: MIT.

23758283.title: Replication package for: "Farmers' beliefs about the impacts of a CO2e tax on agriculture and their acceptance of the tax: A randomized survey experiment".
23758283.description: This contains replication materials for the paper, "Farmers’ beliefs about the impacts of a CO2e tax on agriculture and their acceptance of the tax: A randomized survey experiment" (Food Policy, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.foodpol.2026.103214). The materials include anonymized data, Stata code, a variable codebook, and a README with instructions to reproduce all empirical results reported in the article and appendix.

23777010.title: Replication data and code for "Who Gets to Coproduce? Frontline Discretion and the Interpretation of Client Performance Information"

23792229.title: Data and Code for: Collective Efficacy, Emigration Intention, and Political Participation Intention among University Students after Nepal's 2025 Youth Movement: A Survey Experiment
23792229.description: This record contains the de-identified data, analysis code, and reproduced tables and figures for the article "Collective Efficacy, Emigration Intention, and Political Participation Intention among University Students after Nepal's 2025 Youth Movement: A Survey Experiment" (Songwanjing Zhang, School of International Relations and Diplomacy, Beijing Foreign Studies University). Study overview: A single-factor, two-level between-subjects survey experiment (reform-progress vs. reform-stagnation news frame) was embedded in an online cross-sectional survey (Qualtrics) of students enrolled in English-medium programs at three universities in Nepal. Data were collected from March to June 2026. The valid analytic sample comprises 930 participants (474 in the progress group, 456 in the stagnation group). Measures include perceived reform progress (manipulation check), collective efficacy, hope for the nation's future, normative political participation intention, emigration intention, behavioral preparation for emigration, perceived social mobility, subjective socioeconomic status, family migration network, social desirability, and demographic variables. Files: 1. raw_data_collective_efficacy_emigration_participation.xlsx – de-identified participant-level survey data. 2. reproduction_code_collective_efficacy_emigration_participation.R – R script reproducing all analyses reported in the article (R 4.6.1, lavaan 0.7-3). 3. all_tables_and_figures_reproduced.xlsx – output tables and figure data generated by the R script. Records from individuals under 18 were excluded from the analysis and shared data. Ethics: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Beijing Foreign Studies University (approval no. BFSU-IRB-2026-07; January 8, 2026).

23809259.title: Dataset kuisioner pakar dan perhitungan BWM untuk seleksi pemasok lokal proyek EPC di Riau
23809259.description: This dataset supports the paper “A Hierarchical Best-Worst Method for Weighting Resilience and Compliance Criteria in Local Supplier Selection for EPC Projects in Riau, Indonesia”. It contains the anonymized questionnaire responses of seven practitioners of an Indonesian EPC contractor and the complete Best-Worst Method (BWM) calculations: individual pillar weights with input-based consistency ratios, aggregated pillar weights, within-pillar weights, the global weights of eight sub-criteria, and a sensitivity check in which C8 (legal and tax compliance) is treated as a pass/fail gate. Version 1.1: the EPC experience category of three experts was corrected to “5–10 years” after re-confirmation with the respondents, and two sensitivity-analysis sheets with charts were added (3_Uji C8 Gate and 4_Uji Leave One Out). All BWM inputs and weights are unchanged from version 1.0. See 1.1. README.txt for details.

23827089.title: Data and Code for: Framing Sport Psychology Services and Mental Health Help-Seeking Intentions Among Chinese DanceSport Students: A Randomized Vignette Experiment
23827089.description: This dataset contains the de-identified data and analysis code for the study “Framing Sport Psychology Services and Mental Health Help-Seeking Intentions Among Chinese DanceSport Students: A Randomized Vignette Experiment.” The study used a two-group between-subjects vignette experiment embedded in an online survey. DanceSport students from nine universities in Shanghai, China, were randomly assigned to read a description of a sport psychology service framed either as performance enhancement or as mental health support. Data were collected from April to July 2026. Of the 812 participants who completed the survey, 636 were retained for analysis after the pre-specified exclusion rules were applied. Outcomes include help-seeking intentions for a psychological distress scenario and a performance problem scenario, anticipated stigma, trait help-seeking stigma, service credibility, a manipulation check, and a behavioral measure (clicking a link to the university counseling center page). Files: Raw_data_sport_psychology_service_framing.xlsx: de-identified participant-level raw data with variable descriptions. Paper_tables_and_figures.xlsx: data underlying all tables and figures in the manuscript. reproduce_tables_and_figures.R: R script that reproduces all tables and figures reported in the manuscript. How to reproduce: Requires R ( https://www.r-project.org ); RStudio is optional. Required packages are listed at the top of the script. Put all three files in the same folder. Open reproduce_tables_and_figures.R, set the working directory to that folder, and install any missing packages. Run the script. Its output should match the manuscript and Paper_tables_and_figures.xlsx. No personally identifying information was collected. Please cite the associated article when using these data.

23922413.title: Replication package for "When do contingent valuation and discrete choice experiments converge? Evidence from a meta-analysis of environmental valuation studies"
23922413.description: Replication package for the article “When do contingent valuation and discrete choice experiments converge? Evidence from a meta-analysis of environmental valuation studies”. The package contains the dataset of 60 within-study comparisons between contingent valuation and discrete choice experiment estimates of willingness to pay, drawn from 40 environmental valuation studies that satisfy an explicit four-condition comparability rule; the verification log that records every extracted value against its primary source; the design coding sheet with the verbatim evidence behind every classification; a codebook of 70 entries; and two independent implementations of the analysis, in Stata and in R, which are cross-checked coefficient by coefficient. No primary survey data were collected: every value is extracted from a published study.
keywords: contingent valuation; discrete choice experiments; willingness to pay; convergent validity; meta-analysis; stated preferences; environmental valuation; replication package.

23971008.title: Consumer Acceptance of Biofortified Iron Beans in Kenya: A Willingness-to-Pay and Choice Experiment Approach
23971008.description: Biofortification is increasingly being recognized as a cost-effective strategy for addressing micronutrient deficiencies, particularly among vulnerable populations. Biofortified Iron Beans (BIBs) offer a promising approach to reducing iron deficiency. This dataset comprises survey data from 561 bean consumers and producers in Nairobi and Bomet, Kenya, collected between April and June 2024. The study examines consumer awareness, knowledge, preferences, and acceptance of BIBs, guided by an extended Theory of Planned Behavior framework. The survey captures household characteristics, bean consumption patterns, nutrition knowledge, attitudes, subjective norms, perceived behavioral control, and purchase intentions. It also incorporates contingent valuation and discrete choice experiments to assess consumers' willingness to pay for BIBs and their preferences for different product attributes. Additional data cover household income, dietary diversity, gender dynamics, and household decision-making. The anonymized dataset, available in CSV format, provides opportunities for research on consumer demand for biofortified crops, nutrition-sensitive food systems, and strategies for promoting the uptake of nutrient-rich foods in Kenya.

23990275.title: Reference-system dependence in youth fitness assessment: transparency materials
23990275.description: This dataset contains transparency materials supporting the manuscript “Same performance, different classification: Reference-system dependence in youth fitness assessment in Colombia”. It provides aggregate results, analysis and figure-generation code, published reference-table mappings, a data dictionary, a change log, and computational checks for a paired comparison of FUPRECOL and FitBack classifications in 31 schoolchildren aged 9-12 years. Version 4 corrects the chance-agreement formula previously used for linearly weighted Gwet AC2 and regenerates the associated paired BCa confidence intervals; the primary mean percentile shifts and reclassification counts are unchanged. It also documents the P70/P75 ambiguity in the Colombian handgrip source and the implemented upper-tail bounds. No participant-level data table is deposited because of re-identification risk in a small sample of minors. This is an analysis-transparency record, not a manuscript preprint.

24012048.title: What Data Consistency Can and Cannot Verify: preregistration, analysis code, run manifests and summary statistics
24012048.description: Preregistration (all dated revisions, 1–7 with addenda), analysis code, run manifests, the per-condition outcome-interpretation table, summary statistics, retraining records and the retrained reconstruction weights for the manuscript "What Data Consistency Can and Cannot Verify: A Preregistered Evaluation of Deep-Learning MRI Reconstruction Across Architectures and Applications" (submitted to Medical Physics , 2026). Version 2.0.0 : the unrolled (VarNet) and post-processing (U-Net) representatives were retrained on the fastMRI training split only (knee and brain), because the public leaderboard checkpoints used in the first execution had been trained on the validation split from which all evaluation cases are drawn; the confirmatory experiments were re-executed once with the retrained weights (preregistration revision 7). The four retrained state_dict files are deposited as separate files with SHA256. The first execution with the public checkpoints (version 1.1.0) is retained in full inside the archive, since the paired comparison of the two runs is reported as an exploratory natural experiment on evaluation-set memorisation. A post-processing inference normalisation error found after the first retrained run was corrected and that arm re-executed once; the affected run is also retained. Knee cohort (fastMRI, n = 69 cases, 5,796 trials) and an independent, separately preregistered brain replication (n = 41 cases, 3,444 trials). Three reconstruction families (image-domain post-processing U-Net and unrolled VarNet with a learned soft data-consistency update, both retrained on the training split; public HFS-SDE diffusion) under matched acceleration, denoising and super-resolution forward problems; lesion-level error decomposed into measured and null-space parts; data-consistency residual as a failure predictor; architecture-stratified conformal bounds within prespecified lesion ROIs. Not included: raw fastMRI k-space data, download links, or third-party pretrained weights (public fastMRI checkpoints, HFS-SDE). Raw data are available from the NYU fastMRI Initiative under its data-use agreement; fastMRI+ annotations are public (MIT). Code is MIT-licensed (LICENSE file inside the archive); preregistration documents, result tables and figures are CC BY 4.0. See README.md in the archive for the layout, column definitions and reproduction steps.

24023805.title: Practice-Based Faculty Development for English-Medium Instruction: Public Aggregate Dataset, Instruments and Analysis Code
24023805.description: This repository contains supplementary research materials associated with the manuscript Practice-Based Faculty Development for English-Medium Instruction: An Exploratory Mixed-Methods Study of Pedagogical Self-Efficacy and Perceived Constraints . The study presents an exploratory mixed-methods evaluation of a 30-hour practice-based faculty-development course designed to support university lecturers teaching disciplinary subjects through English at a public technical university in Poland. The research employed a single-group pretest–posttest design combining quantitative questionnaire data with qualitative reflections on participants' professional-development goals and perceived outcomes. Fifteen lecturers participated in the course. Complete matched data were available for eight participants for pedagogical self-efficacy and six for perceived EMI constraints. The quantitative findings indicated an increase in reported pedagogical self-efficacy (mean change = +0.86; exact Wilcoxon p = .016). Perceived EMI constraints decreased on average (mean change = −0.50), although the paired comparison was statistically inconclusive (p = .156). Qualitative findings indicated a broadening of participants' reported priorities from predominantly language-related concerns towards pedagogical preparedness. Repository contents The deposited materials include: Aggregate quantitative results, including composite and item-level summaries. Aggregate qualitative findings and the qualitative coding framework. Polish-language questionnaire documentation and English translations. A detailed variable dictionary and scoring specifications. Python analysis scripts and a Google Colab notebook. Documentation of analytical procedures, computational requirements and reproducibility limitations. Data availability and confidentiality Only aggregate quantitative and qualitative results are publicly released. Participant-level questionnaire responses, individual longitudinal trajectories, identifiable background information and verbatim qualitative statements have been excluded because of the potential risk of re-identification within the small institutional cohort. The deposited analysis code documents the analytical procedure, but independent recalculation of participant-level statistical tests requires access to the restricted original data. The postprogram Polish questionnaire included in this repository is a documented reconstruction rather than a preserved historical copy of the administered instrument. Purpose The repository aims to support research transparency, methodological scrutiny and the reuse of research instruments and analytical approaches in studies of English-medium instruction, academic language development and higher-education faculty development, subject to applicable rights and permissions.

24079949.title: Swedish Consumers' Preferences for Tofu Sustainability Characteristics: A Choice Experiment with Information Treatments — Data, Questionnaires and Model Output
24079949.description: Replication data, questionnaires and model output for the article Swedish Consumers’ Preferences for Tofu Sustainability Characteristics: A Choice Experiment with Information Treatments , German Journal of Agricultural Economics (GJAE). Abstract: For achieving a higher share of plant-based proteins in the diets of people in high-income countries, a better understanding of consumers’ preferences for meat alternatives is needed. Using a choice experiment with around 1,400 Swedish consumers, we investigate preferences for local and organic tofu and examine the effect on preferences when providing information about different aspects of tofu consumption (health, environment, culinary). While we do not find any effects of information on preferences, a latent class analysis indicates the existence of heterogeneous preference classes with a substantial share of consumers willing to pay for tofu and for sustainability attributes. Contents. Survey data ( .xlsx ), the English and Swedish questionnaires, a screencast of the survey instrument, and the estimated model output ( modeloutput.zip , folder structure preserved). See MANIFEST.md for the full file list with original OSF paths and md5 checksums. Provenance. Migrated from the OSF project osf.io/a986e , which becomes read-only in February 2027. The preregistration remains on OSF at osf.io/gvxkt . Analysis code: github.com/sagebiej/GJAE_tofu . Version 2 (November 2026). 24086772.title: Replication data: Estimating Recreation Benefits of Avoiding Blue-Green Algae and Red Tide in South Florida
24086772.description: Replication data for “Estimating Recreation Benefits of Avoiding Blue-Green Algae and Red Tide in South Florida” (Journal of Outdoor Recreation and Tourism, submitted). The data come from a four-wave stated preference survey of people planning an outdoor recreation trip in South Florida, fielded on the Dynata panel from April 2024 to March 2025. 24089505.title: Replication Data and Code for "Belief Correction, Approval News, and Irreversible Investment: A Model of Oil and Gas Project Development.
24089505.description: This deposit contains the data and code supporting Belief Correction, Approval News, and Irreversible Investment: A Model of Oil and Gas Project Development . The paper develops a behavioural dynamic stochastic general equilibrium model in which oil and gas producers make project-start and preparation decisions before receiving accurate technical feedback. The numerical exercises separate the effect of correcting readiness beliefs after investment commitments have been made from the response to news about future permit approvals. The replication archive contains three components: Theoretical model and simulations. Model equations, calibration files, steady-state solutions, and MATLAB/Dynare and Python code for the theoretical impulse responses, early- and late-correction transitions, and benchmark and sensitivity comparisons. Mixed-frequency VAR. Estimation inputs, data-processing and estimation code, and saved results for January 2001 through December 2024. The analysis combines monthly U.S. offshore permit approvals, national oil- and gas-directed rig counts, and macroeconomic and financial indicators with quarterly real private investment and government purchases. The archive covers the benchmark, the approval-date screen, and the specifications that separately add conventional and AI-based geopolitical risk. It includes posterior impulse-response summaries and the paired comparison of oil- and gas-directed drilling responses. Argos offshore project chronology. A source-linked chronology and code linking company disclosures and federal well records to document how earlier investment commitments carried into production after a schedule revision. The accompanying README describes the directory structure, software requirements and commands needed to reproduce the analysis. The archive includes saved numerical results for comparison with regenerated outputs. Large posterior draw files can be regenerated using the supplied estimation code. Source documentation identifies the original data providers and records the transformations used to construct the estimation inputs. Third-party materials are subject to their original terms. The VAR provides suggestive evidence on anticipatory drilling. The Argos chronology illustrates the persistence of earlier commitments. The implications of mistaken readiness beliefs and the timing of their correction are derived from the theoretical model.

24091682.title: Taste-based conjoint for fruit flies

24138016.title: Replication package for "Climate change perceptions, vineyard structure and the compensation required to adapt: a choice experiment with Etna winegrowers (Italy)"
24138016.description: This deposit contains the data and code that reproduce every table and figure of the article Signorello G. and Giuffrida L. (2026), “Climate change perceptions, vineyard structure and the compensation required to adapt: a choice experiment with Etna winegrowers (Italy)”. The study surveyed 120 winegrowers of the Etna Controlled Designation of Origin (Sicily, Italy), more than a third of the 346 registered with its Consortium, recording perceptions of climate change and adaptation practices alongside a discrete choice experiment on packages of adaptation measures for existing vineyards, compensated by an annual payment per hectare. Contents. data/ : the survey file, the two derived files on which every estimate is computed, the variable codebook, the GIS layer of the four slope sectors and the vineyard exposure file. python/ : the reference implementation in twelve scripts, from data preparation and the main analysis to the figures, the robustness checks, the dependence structure of the false discovery rate correction, the minimum detectable effect of the binary models, vineyard exposure, the coherence of choices with stated intentions, the size and power of the Swait-Louviere test and the trends of the observed climate series. R/ and stata/ : the same analysis in R and in Stata, plus a cross-check of the choice models with Apollo. climate/ : the WorldClim-derived climatologies and annual series used to characterise the denomination. output/ : all results, tables and figures produced by the three languages. Reproducibility. The three implementations were run and agree: multinomial logit log-likelihood −435.799, two-class latent class −393.484, latent class with membership covariates −383.556. Penalised profile-likelihood inference for the Firth logits matches between Python and R to the last printed digit on all 204 coefficients; the Poisson models with HC3 standard errors and offset match to the sixth decimal; the latent class willingness-to-accept estimates agree to about 0.2 EUR per hectare. 24183055.description: Numerical data and code supporting the study "External calibration constraints on localization reliability and measurement budgets for concealed pipe sources". 4009671.title: Estimating the costs of new mobility travel options: monetary and non-monetary factors
4009671.description: UC Davis researchers have developed a cost model of travel choices that individuals make related to urban vehicle travel. These choices can include deciding to own, ride in, and drive a private vehicle or use pooled or solo ridesourcing (e.g., Uber). The model considers both monetary and non-monetary factors that affect travel choice. Monetary factors include the costs of purchasing, maintaining, and fueling different types of privately owned vehicles; and the cost of using ridesourcing services. Non-monetary (or "hedonic") factors include travel time, parking time/inconvenience, willingness to drive or be a passenger in a driven or automated vehicle, and willingness to travel with strangers. The travel choices affected by these factors impact broader society through traffic congestion, pollution, greenhouse gas emissions, accidents, etc. and thus may be an important focus of policy. This report reviews recent literature, considers factors affecting travel choices, and reports, on a conjoint pilot survey or stated preferences. Finally, it considers approaches to apply time value to factors that are not typically associated with specific trips, such as time spent on vehicle maintenance and parking. The results should enable a deeper understanding of the likelihood that individuals will own and use private vehicles or use shared (solo and pooled) ridesourcing, and how automated vehicle services could affect these choices in the future. The study also highlights additional research needs, such as a large scale stated preference study covering more factors than have been included in previous studies.

4069038.title: Data from: Linking land use and the nutritional ecology of herbivores: a case study with the Senegalese locust
4069038.description: 1) Access to high-quality food is a main driver of population dynamics. For herbivores protein and carbohydrates are key nutrients that are notoriously variable in plants and are affected by land use. However, few studies have linked foraging decisions and performance in the laboratory to the nutritional landscape available in the field. 2) Oedaleus senegalensis is a nonmodel locust, a grass-feeder, and the main pest of millet, a subsistence crop in the Sahel. In this study, we examined dietary preference and locust performance across a range of protein:carbohydrate ratios using the Geometric Framework methodology. We then applied a fitness landscape approach to visualize these results with the plant nutrient contents available across four land-use types: millet, groundnut, fallow, and grazed fields. Finally, we contrasted our results with locust distribution in the field. Several locust species ( O. senegalensis included) exhibit density dependent color polymorphism thus we also reported individual coloration (brown or green). 3) We found that O. senegalensis preferred moderately carbohydrate-biased food 1:1.6 protein: carbohydrate ratio. All traits recorded (mass gain, development time, growth rate, molt success, and performance index) were best near that ratio and declined on either side presenting a "hump-shape". Fallow fields contained more plants, particularly grasses, that were both abundant and closer to the optimal protein:carbohydrate ratio recorded from the lab experiments. 4) When we surveyed O. senegalensis abundance and proportion, we found that they were more numerous in the fallow fields. Brown morph individuals, the ones associated with high density, were proportionally more abundant in fallow fields than green individuals. 5) Our study provides evidence that variation in nutritional landscapes—relative to an herbivore's optimal nutrient balance—is a key driver of herbivore population distribution and abundance, and can be used to predict bottom-up effects on herbivore species. protein:carbohydrate ratio recorded from the lab experiments.

4090973.title: Between the Frames - Evaluation of Various Motion Interpolation Algorithms to Improve 360° Video Quality
4090973.description: With the increasing availability of 360° video content, it becomes important to provide smoothly playing videos of high quality for end users. For this reason, we compare the influence of different Motion Interpolation (MI) algorithms on 360° video quality. After conducting a pre-test with 12 video experts in [3], we found that MI is a useful tool to increase the QoE (Quality of Experience) of omnidirectional videos. As a result of the pretest, we selected three suitable MI algorithms, namely ffmpeg Motion Compensated Interpolation (MCI), Butterflow and Super- SloMo. Subsequently, we interpolated 15 entertaining and realworld omnidirectional videos with a duration of 20 seconds from 30 fps (original framerate) to 90 fps, which is the native refresh rate of the HMD used, the HTC Vive Pro. To assess QoE, we conducted two subjective tests with 24 and 27 participants. In the first test we used a Modified Paired Comparison (M-PC) method, and in the second test the Absolute Category Rating (ACR) approach. In the M-PC test, 45 stimuli were used and in the ACR test 60. Results show that for most of the 360° videos, the interpolated versions obtained significantly higher quality scores than the lower-framerate source videos, validating our hypothesis that motion interpolation can improve the overall video quality for 360° video. As expected, it was observed that the relative comparisons in the M-PC test result in larger differences in terms of quality. Generally, the ACR method lead to similar results, while reflecting a more realistic viewing situation. In addition, we compared the different MI algorithms and can conclude that with sufficient available computing power Super-SloMo should be preferred for interpolation of omnidirectional videos, while MCI also shows a good performance.

4268587.title: Understanding what women want: eliciting preference for delivery health facility in a rural sub-County in Kenya, a discrete choice experiment
4268587.description: Objective: To identify what women want in a delivery health facility and how they rank the attributes that influence the choice of a place of delivery. Design: A Discrete Choice Experiment was conducted to elicit rural women's preferences for choice of delivery health facility. Data were analyzed using both a conditional logit model to evaluate relative importance of the selected attributes. A mixed multinomial model evaluated how interactions with sociodemographic variables influence the choice of the selected attributes. Setting: Six health facilities in a rural sub-County. Participants: Women aged 18-49 years who had delivered within six weeks. Primary outcome: The DCE required women to select from hypothetical health facility A or B or opt-out alternative. Results: A total of 474 participants were sampled, 466 participants completed the survey (response rate 98%).The attribute with the strongest association with health facility preference was having a kind and supportive healthcare worker (β=1.184, p&lt;0.001), second availability of medical equipment and drug supplies (β=1.073, p&lt;0.001) and third quality of clinical services (β=0.826, p&lt;0.001). Distance, availability of referral services and costs were ranked 4th, 5th and 6th respectively (β=0.457, p&lt;0.001), (β=0.266 p&lt;0.001), and (β=0.000018, p&lt;0.001). The opt-out alternative ranked last suggesting a disutility for home delivery. (β=-0.849, p&lt;0.001). Conclusion: The most highly valued attribute was a process indicator of quality of care followed by technical indicators. Policy makers need to consider women's preferences to inform strategies that are person-centered and lead to improvements in quality of care during delivery.

4321834.title: Communicating risk in human-wildlife interactions: how stories and images move minds
4321834.description: Effectively communicating risk is critical to reducing conflict in human-wildlife interactions. Using a survey experiment fielded in the midst of contentious public debate over flying fox management in urban and suburban areas of Australia, we find that stories with characters (i.e., narratives) are more effective than descriptive information at mobilizing support for different forms of bat management, including legal protection, relocation, and habitat restoration. We use conditional process analysis to show that narratives, particularly with accompanying images, are effective because they cause emotional reactions that influence risk perception, which in turn drives public opinion about strategies for risk mitigation. We find that prior attitudes towards bats matter in how narrative messages are received, in particular in how strongly they generate shifts in affective response, risk perception, and public opinion. Our results suggest that those with warm prior attitudes towards bats report greater support for bat dispersal when they perceive impacts from bats to be more likely, while those with cool priors report greater support for bat protection when they perceive impacts from bats to be more positive, revealing 1) potential opportunities for targeted messaging to boost public buy-in of proposals to manage risks associated with human-wildlife interactions, and 2) potential vulnerabilities to disinformation regarding risk.

4328879.title: Concerns of surrogate decision makers for acute brain injury patients: a US population survey
4328879.description: Objective: To determine whether groups of surrogates for severe acute brain injury (SABI) patients with poor prognosis can be identified based on their prioritization of goals-of-care (GOC) decisional concerns, an online survey of 1588 adults recruited via a probability-based panel representative of the US population was conducted. Methods: Participants acted as a surrogate for a GOC decision for a hypothetical SABI patient and were randomized to one of two prognostic scenarios: the patient likely being left with a range of severe functional disability (SD) or remaining in a vegetative state (VS). Participants prioritized a list of 12 decisional concerns via Best-Worst Scaling. Latent class analysis (LCA) was used to discover decisional groups. Results: The completion rate was 44.6%; data weighting was conducted to mitigate nonresponse bias. For 792 SD respondents, LCA revealed four groups. All groups shared concerns regarding respecting patient wishes and minimizing suffering. The four groups were otherwise distinguished by unique concerns that their members highlighted: an older adult remaining severely disabled (34.4%), family consensus (26.4%), doubt regarding prognostic accuracy (20.7%), and cost of long-term care (18.6%). For the 796 VS respondents, LCA revealed five groups. Four of the five groups had similar concern profiles to the four SD groups. The largest (29.0%) expressed the most prognostic doubt. An additional group (15.8%) prioritized religious concerns. Conclusions: While surrogate decision makers for patients with SABI are concerned with respecting patient wishes and minimizing suffering, certain groups highly prioritize other specific decisional factors. These data can help inform future interventions for supporting decision makers.

4503618.title: Data from: Land cover, individual's age and spatial sorting shape landscape resistance in the invasive frog Xenopus laevis
4503618.description: 1. The description of functional connectivity is based on the quantification of landscape resistance, which represents species-specific movement costs across landscape features. Connectivity models use these costs to identify movement corridors at both individual and population levels and provide management recommendations for populations of conservation interest. Typically, resistance costs assigned to specific land cover types are assumed to be valid for all individuals of the population. Little attention has been paid to intraspecific variation in resistance costs due to age or dispersal syndrome, which may significantly affect model predictions. 2. We quantified resistance costs in an expanding invasive population of the African clawed frog Xenopus laevis in Western France. In this principally aquatic amphibian, juveniles, sub-adults and adults disperse overland. The enhancement of dispersal traits via spatial sorting has been also observed at the range periphery of the population. Resistance costs, and thus connectivity, might vary as a function of life stage and position within the invaded range. 3. We assessed multiple dimensions of functional connectivity. On various land cover types, we measured locomotion, as crossing speed, in different post-metamorphic age classes, and dehydration, sensitivity of locomotion to dehydration, and substrate preference in juveniles. We also tested the effect of the position in the invaded range (core vs. periphery) on individual performances. 4. In juveniles, general trends toward higher resistance costs on grass and lower resistance costs on bare soil and asphalt were observed, although not all experiments provided the same cost configurations. Resistance to locomotion varied between age classes, with adults and subadults facing lower costs than juveniles, particularly when crossing structurally complex land cover types like grass and leaf litter. The position in the range had a minor effect on landscape resistance, and only in the dehydration experiment, where water loss in juveniles was lower at the range periphery. 5. Depicting functional connectivity requires: i) assessing multiple dimensions of behavioural and physiological challenges faced by animals during movement; ii) considering factors, such as age and dispersal syndrome, that may affect movement at both individual and population level. Ignoring this complexity might generate unreliable connectivity models and provide unsupported management recommendations for conservation.

4557572.title: Cartographie des milieux humides et de l'abondance potentielle de la sauvagine dans le Québec forestier à partir de la carte écoforestière du  3e inventaire
4557572.description: Résumé : Les forêts de l’Est de l’Amérique du Nord sont traditionnellement considérées pauvres en milieux humides et on leur accorde donc peu d’importance au point de vue de la conservation de la sauvagine. Toutefois, ces forêts comptent sans aucun doute des concentrations importantes de milieux humides et de sauvagine, qui risquent d’être irréversiblement altérées si elles ne sont pas identifiées et gérées adéquatement. Ce projet avait donc pour but de cartographier les milieux humides et d’eau profonde et de modéliser l’abondance de la sauvagine dans le Québec forestier. En améliorant ainsi nos connaissances sur les particularités régionales des milieux humides et d’eau profonde et sur l’utilisation qu’en fait la sauvagine, il sera possible de développer des stratégies d’aménagement de ces milieux qui soient écologiquement fondées. Le produit final est une base de données intitulée Classification des milieux humides et modélisation de l’abondance de sauvagine dans le Québec forestier. Ce projet couvre la zone de chevauchement des inventaires aériens du Plan Conjoint sur le Canard Noir - Service Canadien de la Faune (PCCN – SCF) (517,000 km 2 ) et de la couverture des cartes écoforestières numériques du 3 e inventaire décennal du Ministère des ressources naturelles et de la faune (MRNF) (584,000 km 2 ). Des applications géomatiques ArcMap ont été développées afin de faciliter l’utilisation et la diffusion de l’information.

4672517.title: Pathways to care and preferences for improving tuberculosis services among tuberculosis patients in Zambia
4672517.description: Background: Delays in the diagnosis of tuberculosis (TB) contribute to a substantial proportion of TB-related mortality, especially among people living with HIV (PLHIV). We sought to characterize the diagnostic journey for HIV-positive and HIV-negative patients with a new TB diagnosis in Zambia, to understand drivers of delay, and characterize their preferences for service characteristics to inform improvements in TB services. Methods: We assessed consecutive adults with newly microbiologically-confirmed TB at two public health treatment facilities in Lusaka, Zambia. We administered a survey to document critical intervals in the TB care pathway (time to initial care-seeking, diagnosis and treatment initiation), identify bottlenecks and their reasons. We quantified patient preferences for a range of characteristics of health services using a discrete choice experiment (DCE) that assessed 7 attributes (distance, wait times, hours of operation, confidentiality, sex of provider, testing incentive, TB test speed and notification method). Results: Among 401 patients enrolled (median age of 34 years, 68.7% male, 46.6% HIV-positive), 60.9% and 39.1% were from a first-level and tertiary hospital, respectively. The median time from symptom onset to receipt of TB treatment was 5.0 weeks (IQR: 3.6-8.0) and was longer among HIV-positive patients seeking care at a tertiary hospital than HIV-negative patients (6.4 vs. 4.9 weeks, p=0.002). The time from symptom onset to initial presentation for evaluation accounted for the majority of time until treatment initiation (median 3.0 weeks, IQR: 1.0-5.0) – an important minority of 11.0% of patients delayed care-seeking >=8 weeks. The DCE found that patients strongly preferred same-day TB test results (relative importance, 37.2%), facilities close to home (18.0%), and facilities with short wait times (16.9%). Patients were willing to travel to a facility up to 7.6 kilometers further away in order to access same-day TB test results. Preferences for improving current TB services did not differ according to HIV-status. Conclusions: Prolonged intervals from TB symptom onset to treatment initiation were common, especially among PLHIV, and were driven by delayed health-seeking. Addressing known barriers to timely diagnosis and incorporating patients' preferences into TB services, including same-day TB test results, may facilitate earlier TB care engagement in high burden settings.

4704891.title: Results and further resources concerning our study concerning revealing biases in news articles
4704891.description: Media bias and its extreme form, fake news, can decisively affect public opinion. Especially when reporting on policy issues, slanted news coverage may strongly influence societal decisions, e.g., in democratic elections. Our paper makes three contributions to address this issue. First, we present a system for bias identification, which combines state-of-the-art methods from natural language understanding. Second, we devise bias-sensitive visualizations to communicate bias in news articles to non-expert news consumers. Third, our main contribution is a large-scale user study that measures bias-awareness in a setting that approximates daily news consumption, e.g., we present respondents with a news overview and individual articles. We not only measure the visualizations' effect on respondents' bias-awareness, but we can also pinpoint the effects to individual components of the visualizations by employing a conjoint design. Our bias-sensitive overviews strongly and significantly increase bias-awareness in respondents. Our study further suggests that our content-driven identification method detects groups of similarly slanted news articles due to substantial biases present in individual news articles. In contrast, the reviewed prior work rather only facilitates the visibility of biases, e.g., by distinguishing left- and right-wing outlets.

4876535.title: Relational values help explain green infrastructure preferences: The case of managing crane habitat in Hokkaido, Japan
4876535.description: The initial purpose of our study was to understand preferences of stakeholders on green infrastructure for flood control using a discrete choice experiment. However, the results of our study included unexpected findings. According to the utility theory of economics, an inexpensive green infrastructure scenario should have been chosen under ceteris paribus conditions, but our results differed from this expectation. Inconsistent results like ours are often interpreted as indicating bias and/or questionnaire design issues. However, our results can be interpreted using relational values. We studied green infrastructure in a large-scale flood control basin in Naganuma, a town in the Hokkaido prefecture in Northern Japan. We conducted a discrete choice experiment with town residents as stakeholders of the green infrastructure. Through the examination of choice and membership parameters of our results, we interpreted that individual identity and place attachment, which are types of relational values, are taken into consideration in the choice situation of the discrete choice experiment. We also found that a notion of social responsibility, which is also a relational value, can help us to understand unexpected findings that cannot be interpreted in terms of economic theory alone. Relational values contribute to our interpretation of preferences related to managing ecosystem services with implications for green infrastructure, culturally significant wildlife, wildlife-related recreation, and flood control.

4908209.title: Survey-Experiment data for "Facts, alternative facts, and fact checking in times of post-truth politics" and the replication code
4908209.description: How effective is fact-checking in countervailing “alternative facts,” i.e., misleading statements by politicians? In a randomized online experiment during the 2017 French presidential election campaign, we subjected subgroups of 2480 French voters to alternative facts by the extreme-right candidate, Marine Le Pen, and/or corresponding facts about the European refugee crisis from official sources. This is the dataset from this experiment. We also include the replication code for the article: Barrera, Oscar, Sergei Guriev, Emeric Henry, and Ekaterina Zhuravskaya. 2020. "Facts, alternative facts, and fact checking in times of post-truth politics." Journal of Public Economics, 182: 104123. DOI:  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpubeco.2019.104123

4931473.title: Data from: Methods to identify and prioritize patient-centered outcomes for use in comparative effectiveness research
4931473.description: Background: We used various methods for identifying and prioritizing patient-centered outcomes (PCOs) for comparative effectiveness research (CER). Methods: We considered potential PCOs ("benefits" and "harms") related to (1) gabapentin for neuropathic pain and (2) quetiapine for bipolar depression. Part 1 (April 2014 to March 2015): we searched for PCO research and core outcome sets (COSs). We conducted electronic searches of bibliographic databases and key websites and examined FDA prescribing information and reports of clinical trials and systematic reviews. We asked patient and clinician co-investigators to identify PCOs. Part 2 (not part of our original study protocol): in 2015, we surveyed members of The TMJ Association, Ltd., a patient group associated with temporomandibular disorders (4130 invitations sent). Participants prioritized (1) the importance of six potential benefits and (2) 21 potential harms selected by the investigators in part 1, using stated preference methods. We calculated descriptive statistics. Results: In part 1, we identified a COS for pain, the Initiative on Methods, Measurement, and Pain Assessment in Clinical Trials (IMMPACT) recommendations. The COS identified several important benefits, but it lacked specific recommendations about which potential harms to include in CER. We did not identify a COS for bipolar depression. Research reports, prescribing information, and patient co-investigators helped identify but not prioritize outcomes. We abandoned our electronic search for PCO research because we found it would be resource-intensive and yield few relevant reports. In part 2, surveying patients was useful for prioritizing PCOs. Members of The TMJ Association, Ltd., completed the survey (N = 746) and successfully prioritized both benefits and harms. Participants did not identify many benefits other than those we identified in part 1; several participants identified additional harms. Conclusions: These exploratory results could inform future research about identifying and prioritizing PCOs. We found that stakeholder co-investigators and research reports contributed to identifying PCOs; surveying a patient group contributed to prioritizing PCOs. Prioritizing potential harms was particularly challenging because there are many more potential harms than potential benefits. Methods for identifying and prioritizing potential benefits for CER might not be appropriate for harms. Further research is needed to determine the generalizability of these results.

4946496.title: Data from: Red and white Chinook salmon: genetic divergence and mate choice
4946496.description: Chinook salmon (Oncorhynchus tshawytscha) exhibit extreme differences in coloration of skin, eggs and flesh due to genetic polymorphisms affecting carotenoid deposition, where colour can range from white to bright red. A sympatric population of red and white Chinook salmon occurs in the Quesnel River, British Columbia, where frequencies of each phenotype are relatively equal. In our study, we examined evolutionary mechanisms responsible for the maintenance of the morphs, where we first tested whether morphs were reproductively isolated using microsatellite genotyping, and second, using breeding trials in seminatural spawning channels, we tested whether colour assortative mate choice could be operating to maintain the polymorphism in nature. Next, given extreme difference in carotenoid assimilation and the importance of carotenoids to immune function, we examined mate choice and selection between colour morphs at immune genes (major histocompatibility complex genes: MHC I-A1 and MHC II-B1). In our study, red and white individuals were found to interbreed, and under seminatural conditions, some degree of colour assortative mate choice (71% of matings) was observed. We found significant genetic differences at both MHC genes between morphs, but no evidence of MHC II-B1-based mate choice. White individuals were more heterozygous at MHC II-B1 compared with red individuals, and morphs showed significant allele frequency differences at MHC I-A1. Although colour assortative mate choice is likely not a primary mechanism maintaining the polymorphisms in the population, our results suggest that selection is operating differentially at immune genes in red and white Chinook salmon, possibly due to differences in carotenoid utilization.

4946561.title: Data from: No mate preference associated with the supergene controlling social organization in Alpine silver ants
4946561.description: Disassortative mating is a powerful mechanism stabilizing polymorphisms at sex chromosomes and other supergenes. The Alpine silver ant, Formica selysi, has two forms of social organization – single‐queen and multiple‐queen colonies – determined by alternate haplotypes at a large supergene. Here, we explore whether mate preference contributes to the maintenance of the genetic polymorphism at the social supergene. With mate choice experiments, we found that females and males mated randomly with respect to social form. Moreover, queens were able to produce offspring irrespective of whether they had mated with a male from the same or the alternative social form. Yet, females originating from single‐queen colonies were more fertile, suggesting that they may be more successful at independent colony founding. We conclude that the pattern of asymmetric assortative mating documented from mature F. selysi colonies in the field is not caused by mate preferences or major genetic incompatibilities between social forms. More generally, we found no evidence that disassortative mate preference contributes to the maintenance of polymorphism at this supergene controlling ant social organization.

4949318.title: Data from: Modifying maternal sleep position in the third trimester of pregnancy with positional therapy: a randomized pilot trial
4949318.description: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate whether the percentage of time spent supine during sleep in the third trimester of pregnancy could be reduced using a positional therapy device (PrenaBelt) compared with a sham device. DESIGN: A double-blind, randomized, sham-controlled, crossover pilot trial. SETTING: Conducted between March 2016 and January 2017, at a single, tertiary-level center in Canada. PARTICIPANTS: Twenty-three participants entered the study. Twenty participants completed the study. Participants were low-risk, singleton, third-trimester pregnant women aged 18 years and older with BMI <35 at the first antenatal appointment for the index pregnancy and without known fetal abnormalities, pregnancy complications, or medical conditions complicating sleep. INTERVENTIONS: A two-night, polysomnography study in a sleep laboratory. Participants were randomized by computer-generated, one-to-one, simple randomization to receive either a the PrenaBelt or a sham-PrenaBelt on the 1st night and were crossed over to the alternate device on the 2nd night. Allocation concealment was by unmarked, security-tinted, sealed envelopes. Participants, the recruiter, and personnel involved in setting up, conducting, scoring, and interpreting the polysomnogram were blinded to allocation. PRIMARY AND SECONDARY OUTCOME MEASURES: The primary outcome was the percentage of time spent supine during sleep. Secondary outcomes included maternal sleep architecture, respiration, self-reported sleep position, and feedback. RESULTS: The median percentage of sleep time supine was reduced from 16.4% on the sham night to 3.5% on the PrenaBelt night (pseudomedian=5.8, p=0.03). We were unable to demonstrate differences in sleep architecture or respiration. Participants underestimated the time they spent sleeping supine by 7.0%, and six (30%) participants indicated they would make changes to the PrenaBelt. There were no harms in this study. CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates that the percentage of sleep time supine during late pregnancy can be significantly reduced via positional therapy. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02377817
